title: Incident correlation & decomposition playbook
body:
Purpose:
This playbook collects a compact, repeatable sequence for investigating production performance regressions when alerts fire or canaries diverge. It is intentionally pragmatic: aim to narrow the hypothesis within 30–90 minutes and collect artifacts for a postmortem.

Quick summary (what to do first):
1) Triage scope: confirm whether the regression is global, per-region, per-customer, or per-model variant.
2) Snapshot metrics: capture P50/P95/P99 latency, token-per-second (system and per-request), batch size distribution, GPU utilization, kernel stalls, and queue length across 5m/1h/24h windows.
3) If canary exists, compute canary-vs-prod diffs for the same time window and workload. Save snapshots.
4) Start a bisect: narrow to commit range or config change window, prioritize config/infra changes before model code.

Investigation checklist (ordered):
- Alert intake: copy alert text, time range, affected clusters, and run_id/sample request ids. Ensure alert contains correlating trace IDs.
- Dashboards to open (minimum):
  - Serving runtime: latency percentiles (P50/P90/P95/P99) by model and route.
  - Request pipeline: prequeue time, slot wait, batch size histogram, request batching rate.
  - GPU hosts: GPU util, GPU memory alloc, kernel time per inference, nvtx timelines.
  - Host metrics: CPU steal, iowait, network errors, disk busy (if on-prem).
  - Autoscaler: recent scale events, pod restarts, placement changes.
  - Cache/KV: cache hit rate, prefix cache warming, cold-starts.

Prometheus/Observability queries (examples):
- P99 latency by model in last 1h:
  histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_latency_seconds_bucket[1h])) by (le, model))
- Average batch size over 5m:
  sum(rate(batch_size_sum[5m])) / sum(rate(batch_size_count[5m]))
- Token throughput (tokens/sec) by node:
  sum(rate(tokens_generated_total[5m])) by (node)
- Kernel time vs memcpy time (GPU host):
  sum(rate(gpu_kernel_time_seconds_total[5m])) by (host) / sum(rate(gpu_memcpy_time_seconds_total[5m])) by (host)

Sampling and artifact capture (what to save):
- Time-series snapshots (export PNGs/CSV) for the 15m before alert, during, and 15m after.
- Representative request trace(s) that show the tail spike: include full span logs, model input size, and token count.
- Example requests (input text) for local repro.
- Node-level perf profile: perf record --call-graph dwarf -p <pid> -g -o perf.data (10s steady-state), or Nsight capture if GPU timeline necessary.
- GPU sampling via CUPTI/Nsight or ncu: ncu --target-processes all --csv -o ncu_capture <cmd>.

Bisect guidance (code/config timeline):
1) If regression aligns with a known deploy time, start by rolling back that deploy in a canary or staging environment.
2) If a range of commits is suspected, use binary search on commit range with a minimal synthetic load that reproduces tail behavior. Keep tests deterministic (same seeds, same input set).
3) When config changes are present (drivers, kernel, CUDA, infra), prefer testing config rollbacks first — they are common causes for sudden performance shifts.
4) Record each bisect step in notes: commit/config tested, snapshot links, verdict (repro / not repro).

Canary comparison technique:
- Run the same request set against canary and prod with identical traffic shaping (same QPS and arrival jitter).
- Produce diff metrics: delta(P95), delta(batch-size-mean), delta(queue-wait).
- For each divergence, correlate with system metrics on the serving hosts (GPU kernel times, memcpy, host CPU steal).

Profiling heuristics and hotspots to watch for:
- Blocking memcpy/PCIe saturation: look for memcpy times growing relative to kernel time and queued NVLINK traffic.
- Batch packing regressions: if mean batch size drops or variance spikes, check recent batching code and input token distribution changes.
- KV/prefix cache misses: rising cold-start fraction often predicts token-level latency spikes.
- GC/allocator pauses on host: long CPU syscalls or unexpected sweeps can push scheduling delays into tail latency.
- Model runtime changes: new ops or fused kernels may increase per-token compute; check selected kernel versions and quantization artifacts.

Quick triage decision matrix (example):
- If canary==healthy & prod==regressed -> likely infra/config or traffic-targeting bug; escalate to infra and check placement/traffic routing.
- If canary==regressed & prod==regressed -> likely code/model change; prioritize revert or hotfix PR.
- If only one customer affected -> check routing rules, feature flags, and model pins for that customer.

Communication / incident notes template (to paste to Slack/incidents):
- Summary: short one-liner of impact and scope.
- Current status: triage actions done and artifacts collected.
- Next steps: who is owning bisect, profiling, and customer comms.
- Key data: P95 delta, example trace id(s), links to dashboards and perf captures.

Postmortem collection (if regression confirmed):
- Attach: final hypothesis, evidence (profiles, diffs), timeline of deploys/config changes, and RCA owner.
- Action items: code rollbacks, additional test harnesses (e.g., automated canary comparisons for batch size), alert tuning.

Practical tips / gotchas:
- Don’t trust absolute timestamps across services; align on a single monotonic time (trace timestamps) when correlating.
- Small changes in request routing can look like performance regressions; confirm request distribution is identical when comparing canary/prod.
- Synthetic loads can hide intermittency; include jitter and multi-model mixes in repro attempts.

Short checklist for the first 30 minutes:
- [ ] Capture alert context (time range, sample ids).
- [ ] Export P50/P95/P99 and batch histograms for 1h/24h.
- [ ] Run one representative perf capture (host and GPU) on an affected node.
- [ ] Run canary vs prod diff on a fixed request set.
- [ ] Kick off bisect if a deploy or config change window is identified.

Owner notes: keep this doc minimal and link to deeper runbooks for perf tooling (perf, ncu, Nsight) and to the canonical canary diff notebook. If you add steps or queries that helped you find a regression, paste them here so the next investigator is faster.
